name: Cyber-Physical & Autonomous Vehicle Security
description: Security of cyber-physical systems, ICS/SCADA, robotics, drones, and autonomous/connected vehicles.

uss.narrative:
The earliest USENIX Security work in this area zeroed in on a recurring theme: cyber-physical systems trust their sensors, and that trust is exploitable. "BlackIoT: IoT Botnet of High Wattage Devices Can Disrupt the Power Grid" (USENIX 2018) showed that a botnet of high-wattage appliances could destabilize the power grid by manipulating demand, while "All Your GPS Are Belong To Us: Towards Stealthy Manipulation of Road Navigation Systems" (USENIX 2018) and "Injected and Delivered: Fabricating Implicit Control over Actuation Systems by Spoofing Inertial Sensors" (USENIX 2018) demonstrated that spoofing the physical signals a system depends on (GPS, inertial sensors) could quietly hijack its decisions. The common insight was that the attack surface lives in the physical channel, not just the software.

From 2019 onward the field both broadened across domains and matured toward systematic defense. Vehicle internals and adjacent infrastructure got attention with "CANvas: Fast and Inexpensive Automotive Network Mapping" (USENIX 2019) and "Losing the Car Keys: Wireless PHY-Layer Insecurity in EV Charging" (USENIX 2019), while "RVFuzzer: Finding Input Validation Bugs in Robotic Vehicles through Control-Guided Testing" (USENIX 2019) brought principled fuzzing to robotic-vehicle control software, and "Not Everything is Dark and Gloomy: Power Grid Protections Against IoT Demand Attacks" (USENIX 2019) answered the 2018 grid attack with concrete protections. The 2020 cohort marks the field's pivot to machine-learning perception as the new battleground: "Towards Robust LiDAR-based Perception in Autonomous Driving" (USENIX 2020) proved black-box sensor attacks could fool LiDAR perception, while "SAVIOR: Securing Autonomous Vehicles with Robust Physical Invariants" (USENIX 2020) and "From Control Model to Program: Investigating Robotic Aerial Vehicle Accidents with MAYDAY" (USENIX 2020) pushed physics-based invariants and accident forensics as systematic defenses.

The early 2020s show a clear split between sharper perception attacks and architecture-level defenses. On the attack side, "Too Good to Be Safe: Tricking Lane Detection in Autonomous Driving with Crafted Perturbations" (USENIX 2021), "Rolling Colors: Adversarial Laser Exploits against Traffic Light Recognition" (USENIX 2022), and "TPatch: A Triggered Physical Adversarial Patch" (USENIX 2023) kept finding new ways to deceive vision pipelines, and "An Experimental Study of GPS Spoofing and Takeover Attacks on UAVs" (USENIX 2022) carried the 2018 spoofing thread into real-world drone takeover. On the defense side, "HAWatcher: Semantics-Aware Anomaly Detection for Appified Smart Homes" (USENIX 2021) and "M2MON: Building an MMIO-based Security Reference Monitor for Unmanned Vehicles" (USENIX 2021) built reference monitors and semantics-aware anomaly detection, while fuzzing reached industrial control with "ICSFuzz" (USENIX 2021).

By 2023 the area had widened again to include the human and integrity layers. "That Person Moves Like A Car: Misclassification Attack Detection for Autonomous Systems Using Spatiotemporal Consistency" (USENIX 2023) and "ARI: Attestation of Real-time Mission Execution Integrity" (USENIX 2023) reflect a shift from finding attacks to verifying that perception and mission execution stay trustworthy, and "Exploring User Reactions and Mental Models Towards Perceptual Manipulation Attacks in Mixed Reality" (USENIX 2023) signals the field's expansion into AR/VR and human perception. Across roughly five years the area travelled from "your sensors can be spoofed" to a mature agenda spanning physical-signal attacks, ML-perception robustness, runtime monitoring, and execution-integrity attestation.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work here treats cyber-physical security as a problem of protecting infrastructure and industrial plants. "Exposing Congestion Attack on Emerging Connected Vehicle based Traffic Signal Control" (NDSS 2018) showed that a single spoofed vehicle could jam a whole intersection, and the 2019 cohort turned to defending industrial and grid systems: "A Systematic Framework to Generate Invariants for Anomaly Detection in Industrial Control Systems" (NDSS 2019) mined physical invariants to catch ICS tampering, while "RFDIDS: Radio Frequency-based Distributed Intrusion Detection System for the Power Grid" (NDSS 2019) and "DIAT: Data Integrity Attestation for Resilient Collaboration of Autonomous Systems" (NDSS 2019) extended the same detect-and-attest mindset to power grids and collaborating robots. Even DNA synthesizers came under scrutiny in "Oligo-Snoop" (NDSS 2019), signaling how broadly "cyber-physical" was being read.

Around 2020-2021 the focus moved onto the vehicle itself and its internal buses and sensors. A run of automotive papers — "EASI: Edge-Based Sender Identification" (NDSS 2020), "Hold the Door! Fingerprinting Your Car Key" (NDSS 2020), "Automated Cross-Platform Reverse Engineering of CAN Bus Commands" (NDSS 2020), and "Evading Voltage-Based Intrusion Detection on Automotive CAN" (NDSS 2021) — mapped both attacks and defenses on the CAN bus and keyless entry, while "Metamorph" (NDSS 2020) showed inaudible commands surviving over the air. In parallel, a distinct thread began treating robotic vehicles as software systems to be tested systematically: "PGFUZZ: Policy-Guided Fuzzing for Robotic Vehicles" (NDSS 2021) and later "RVPLAYER" (NDSS 2022) brought fuzzing and forensic replay to drones and rovers.

By 2022-2024 the center of gravity shifted to the perception stack of autonomous systems. "Fooling the Eyes of Autonomous Vehicles" (NDSS 2022) and "Too Afraid to Drive" (NDSS 2022) attacked traffic-sign recognition and driving-planning logic, while a wave of physical sensor-injection work — "SemperFi" anti-spoofing GPS for UAVs (NDSS 2022), "Paralyzing Drones via EMI Signal Injection" (NDSS 2023), "Un-Rocking Drones: Foundations of Acoustic Injection Attacks" (NDSS 2023), "MetaWave" against mmWave sensing (NDSS 2023), and "Invisible Reflections" using IR lasers on traffic signs (NDSS 2024) — established that the analog front-end of a sensor is the real attack surface. V2X security matured in the same window with practical crypto work like "When Cryptography Needs a Hand: Practical Post-Quantum Authentication for V2V" (NDSS 2024).

The most recent work consolidates these threads and pushes into new domains. Sensor spoofing is now stress-tested for real-world plausibility in "On the Realism of LiDAR Spoofing Attacks against Autonomous Driving Vehicle at High Speed and Long Distance" (NDSS 2025) and extended to imaging with "GhostShot" (NDSS 2025) and "The Heat is On" on thermal perception (NDSS 2026), while "SoK: Understanding the Fundamentals and Implications of Sensor Out-of-band Vulnerabilities" (NDSS 2026) systematizes the whole decade of injection attacks. The 2026 slate also shows the field broadening back out to industrial and aerospace targets and adopting new tooling: LLM-driven and dependency-guided fuzzing in "An LLM-Driven Fuzzing Framework for Detecting Logic Instruction Bugs in PLCs" and "ADGFUZZ" (both NDSS 2026), state-machine recovery in "Discovering Blind-Trust Vulnerabilities in PLC Binaries," and entirely new frontiers in "HoneySat" satellite honeypots, "Unknown Target" attacks on aircraft collision avoidance (TCAS), and "FlyTrap" against camera-based target tracking (all NDSS 2026) — a field that began by defending traffic lights now spanning drones, satellites, aircraft, and the full autonomy sensing-to-planning pipeline.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this collection framed cyber-physical security as a problem of trusting the physical layer that classical infosec ignores. Two 2018 S&P papers set the tone from opposite ends: "Learning from Mutants: Using Code Mutation to Learn and Monitor Invariants of a Cyber-Physical System" (S&P 2018) treated a plant as a controller-plus-process whose normal behavior could be learned as invariants and monitored for tampering, while "Crowd-GPS-Sec: Leveraging Crowdsourcing to Detect and Localize GPS Spoofing Attacks" (S&P 2018) attacked the sensing side, showing that a critical navigation input could be forged and then caught by cross-checking many receivers. That split — defend the process logic vs. defend the sensors feeding it — organizes much of what follows. Follow-on 2019 work pushed both threads: "Security of GPS/INS Based On-road Location Tracking Systems" (S&P 2019) showed spoofing survives sensor fusion, "Towards Automated Safety Vetting of PLC Code in Real-World Plants" (S&P 2019) scaled the invariant idea to real industrial controllers, and "Drones' Cryptanalysis - Smashing Cryptography with a Flicker" (S&P 2019) opened the drone attack surface.

Around 2020 the field matured from one-off demonstrations into systematization and detection theory. "SoK: A Minimalist Approach to Formalizing Analog Sensor Security" (S&P 2020) gave the community a shared vocabulary for transduction attacks that inject signals below the digital layer, and "Detection of Electromagnetic Interference Attacks on Sensor Systems" (S&P 2020) and "OAT: Attesting Operation Integrity of Embedded Devices" (S&P 2020) built defenses for interference and for embedded execution integrity respectively. The autonomous-vehicle era then arrived forcefully with "Invisible for both Camera and LiDAR: Security of Multi-Sensor Fusion based Perception in Autonomous Driving Under Physical-World Attacks" (S&P 2021, by far the most cited here), which broke the reassuring assumption that fusing cameras and LiDAR is inherently safe. Sensor-level adversarial machine learning bloomed alongside it in "Poltergeist: Acoustic Adversarial Machine Learning against Cameras and Computer Vision" (S&P 2021), while "CANNON" (S&P 2021) showed automotive bus attacks needing no malicious hardware.

From 2022 onward the venue broadened across every cyber-physical domain at once: robotic-swarm logic flaws ("SWARMFLAWFINDER", S&P 2022) and automated patching ("PGPatch", S&P 2022), real-time availability guarantees ("RT-TEE", S&P 2022), and exposed ICS infrastructure ("Exposed Infrastructures", S&P 2022). The AV perception attack arms race deepened with "PLA-LiDAR: Physical Laser Attacks against LiDAR-based 3D Object Detection" (S&P 2023) and radar spoofing in "mmSpoof" (S&P 2023), answered defensively by certified robustness in "ObjectSeeker" (S&P 2023). Grid and ICS security also grew more empirical and threat-model-honest, in "Shedding Light on Inconsistencies in Grid Cybersecurity" (S&P 2023), "Scaphy" (S&P 2023), and "PCSPOOF" (S&P 2023). A notable 2024 pivot was consolidation and realism: "A Systematic Study of Physical Sensor Attack Hardness" (S&P 2024) asked which sensor attacks are actually practical, and "A Tale of Two Industroyers" (S&P 2024) and "Revisiting Automotive Attack Surfaces" (S&P 2024) grounded the field in real malware and practitioner experience.

The most recent work shows the frontier splintering into new physical surfaces and new platforms. Metaverse and wearable threats appear in "BPSniff: Continuously Surveilling Private Blood Pressure Information in the Metaverse via Unrestricted Inbuilt Motion Sensors" (S&P 2025) and "From Virtual Touch to Tesla Command" (S&P 2024), latency itself becomes an attack vector in "Investigating Physical Latency Attacks Against Camera-Based Perception" (S&P 2025), and even data-center cooling is weaponized in "AquaSonic" (S&P 2024). The 2026 papers make the trajectory clear: attacks on autonomous perception grow more surgical in "Weaponizing Reflectivity for Pointcloud Deception with Forged Invisible Geometries" (S&P 2026) and "Banshee: Target Switch Attacks on Gimbal-Stabilized Visual Tracking Systems via Acoustic Injection" (S&P 2026), ICS testing goes physics-aware and black-box in "Fuzzing the Physical Space" (S&P 2026), and connected-vehicle software joins the fold in "BACHunter: Detecting Broken Access Control Vulnerabilities in Intelligent Connected Vehicles" (S&P 2026). The area now spans the full stack — from analog transduction through perception models to connected-vehicle web APIs — with attack and defense advancing in tandem.

ccs.narrative:
Cyber-physical and autonomous vehicle security at CCS has evolved from control-system anomaly detection to adversarial sensor attacks and AV-stack fuzzing. The 2018 cohort established control-invariant defense as a principled approach: Detecting Attacks Against Robotic Vehicles: A Control Invariant Approach (CCS 2018) derived physical-law-based invariants to detect attacks deviating from expected dynamics, and Truth Will Out: Departure-Based Process-Level Detection of Stealthy Attacks on Control Systems (CCS 2018) generalized this to ICS. Scission (CCS 2018) applied the same principle to automotive CAN buses using ECU signal fingerprints.

The 2019 watershed was Adversarial Sensor Attack on LiDAR-based Perception in Autonomous Driving (CCS 2019), which physically spoofed LiDAR to inject phantom obstacles into self-driving pipelines at the highest citation count of any CCS paper in this dataset. Seeing isn't Believing: Towards More Robust Adversarial Attack Against Real World Object Detectors (CCS 2019) extended physical adversarial patches to real-world object detection.

By 2020-2022, attacks diversified to ADAS cameras and autonomous stacks. Phantom of the ADAS: Securing Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems from Split-Second Phantom Attacks (CCS 2020) showed that projecting images onto roadways fools commercial ADAS sensors. I Can See the Light: Attacks on Autonomous Vehicles Using Invisible Lights (CCS 2021) used invisible infrared to inject false inputs, and DriveFuzz: Discovering Autonomous Driving Bugs through Driving Quality-Guided Fuzzing (CCS 2022) brought systematic fuzzing to the full AV software stack.

milestones.title: Detecting Attacks Against Robotic Vehicles: A Control Invariant Approach
milestones.note: Derived physical control invariants from vehicle dynamics to detect cyber attacks on robotic vehicle systems.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this area, clustered around 2018, staked out two fronts that still define the field. On the infrastructure side, BlackIoT: IoT Botnet of High Wattage Devices Can Disrupt the Power Grid (USENIX 2018) showed that a botnet of air conditioners and heaters could be synchronized to destabilize the bulk power grid, turning consumer IoT into a weapon against physical infrastructure. On the vehicle and sensor side, papers like All Your GPS Are Belong To Us (USENIX 2018) and Injected and Delivered (USENIX 2018) demonstrated that the sensors feeding control systems — GPS receivers, inertial units — could be quietly spoofed. Crucially, a defensive idea appeared alongside the attacks: Detecting Attacks Against Robotic Vehicles: A Control Invariant Approach (CCS 2018) and Learning from Mutants (S&P 2018) proposed watching a system's own physics and control model for deviations, seeding the "physical invariant" line of defense that recurs throughout the decade.

The field's center of gravity then shifted hard toward autonomous driving perception. Adversarial Sensor Attack on LiDAR-based Perception in Autonomous Driving (CCS 2019) was the breakout result — with over 600 citations, it showed spoofed laser returns could inject or hide obstacles — and it triggered a multi-year wave: Towards Robust LiDAR-based Perception (USENIX 2020) generalized the attack to a black-box setting, Can We Use Arbitrary Objects to Attack LiDAR Perception (CCS 2021) and PLA-LiDAR (S&P 2023) broadened the physical means, while camera-side work like Phantom of the ADAS (CCS 2020), Poltergeist (S&P 2021), and Fooling the Eyes of Autonomous Vehicles (NDSS 2022) attacked vision instead. The pivotal reframing came with Invisible for both Camera and LiDAR (S&P 2021), which defeated multi-sensor fusion and dismantled the comforting assumption that combining sensors makes perception secure. Defenses matured in parallel: SAVIOR (USENIX 2020) hardened the invariant-monitoring approach across aerial, ground, and sea vehicles, and SoK: A Minimalist Approach to Formalizing Analog Sensor Security (S&P 2020) began putting the analog attack surface on formal footing.

By the early 2020s the community moved from demonstrating individual exploits to systematic discovery and to the industrial-control domain. DriveFuzz (CCS 2022) and RVFuzzer (USENIX 2019) applied guided fuzzing to whole autonomous-driving and robotic-vehicle stacks, while ICS work such as A Systematic Framework to Generate Invariants for Anomaly Detection in Industrial Control Systems (NDSS 2019) and HoneyPLC (CCS 2020) extended detection and deception to SCADA and PLCs. Power-grid research also matured beyond the attack, with Not Everything is Dark and Gloomy (USENIX 2019) characterizing grid protections against IoT demand attacks.

The most recent work, dominated by NDSS 2026, shows the field both consolidating and pushing into new terrain. SoK: Understanding the Fundamentals and Implications of Sensor Out-of-band Vulnerabilities steps back to unify a decade of analog and out-of-band sensor attacks, while a cluster of PLC papers — An LLM-Driven Fuzzing Framework for Detecting Logic Instruction Bugs in PLCs, Discovering Blind-Trust Vulnerabilities in PLC Binaries via State Machine Recovery, and ADGFUZZ for robotic vehicles — mark a clear methodological turn toward LLM-driven and binary-level analysis of industrial logic. At the same time the attack frontier keeps expanding to new physical targets and platforms: The Heat is On probes thermal-camera perception, PhantomMotion injects motion into wireless surveillance, FlyTrap pulls camera-based target-tracking drones off course, HoneySat brings honeypots to satellites, and SECV adds hardware trust anchors to connected vehicles. The throughline from 2018 to 2026 is consistent — every new autonomous sensor or controller becomes an attack surface — but the tooling for both finding and defending against these flaws has grown markedly more systematic.
